source: USDA Cooperative Extension (Cornell, WSU, UC ANR, UF/IFAS, OSU, Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife); SARE Cover Crops field guide; Rodale Encyclopedia of Organic Gardening; USDA-ARS rotation research. Rotation intervals chosen conservatively to break documented pathogen cycles; aggressive rotations may shorten gaps where disease pressure is known to be low.

entries.reason: Verticillium, Fusarium, and early blight pathogens persist in soil for 3+ years. Nightshades are heavy feeders that deplete nitrogen and concentrate the same root-zone pests (root-knot nematode, Colorado potato beetle). A 3-year gap before replanting any nightshade lets pathogen populations crash.
entries.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension; WSU Extension; UC ANR vegetable production guides

entries.reason: Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae), black rot (Xanthomonas), and cabbage root maggot persist in soil for several years; a 2-year minimum gap suppresses pathogen buildup. Brassicas are heavy nitrogen feeders, so a legume rotation slot is ideal.
entries.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension; Penn State Extension

entries.reason: Powdery mildew, bacterial wilt (vectored by cucumber beetle), and squash vine borer overwinter in residue and soil. A 2-year gap reduces beetle and borer carryover. Avoid following malvaceae since okra and cotton share some cucurbit pests in southern systems.

White rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) and onion fly persist in soil for years once established. A 2-year gap minimum, 4+ years if white rot is present. Allium sulfur compounds inhibit legume Rhizobium symbiosis, so avoid planting legumes immediately after alliums in the same bed.

Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium root-nodule symbiosis and leave 50-150 lb residual N/acre behind. Best placed in the rotation slot before heavy-feeding crops (corn, brassicas, nightshades). Self-rotation 2-year minimum to break root-rot pathogens (Fusarium, Aphanomyces) and bean beetles.
entries.source: SARE Cover Crops field guide; Cornell Cooperative Extension

entries.reason: Carrot rust fly (Psila rosae), parsleyworm (Papilio polyxenes), and Alternaria leaf blight build up in beds replanted to apiaceae crops. A 2-year gap breaks the rust fly life cycle and reduces leaf blight inoculum.

Grasses (corn, small grains, cover-crop cereals) break disease cycles for most vegetable families and add high-C residue that improves soil structure. Heavy nitrogen feeders themselves, so best preceded by a legume. Self-rotation tolerable but a 1-year break reduces corn rootworm pressure.
entries.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension; SARE Cover Crops field guide

entries.reason: Cercospora leaf spot, beet curly top virus, and leaf miner (Pegomya hyoscyami) carry over in soil and residue. Beets, chard, spinach, quinoa, and amaranth all share the same pest and disease complex.

Lettuce drop (Sclerotinia minor), downy mildew (Bremia lactucae), and aster yellows phytoplasma build up in successive composite plantings. A 2-year gap minimum, 3+ years where Sclerotinia is endemic.
entries.source: UC ANR lettuce production guide; Cornell Cooperative Extension

entries.reason: Most mint-family herbs are perennials that occupy their bed long-term and do not need annual rotation. Annual basil is the main exception: rotate with any non-mint family to break Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. basilici (basil wilt) which can persist 8+ years in soil.
entries.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension; herb production guides

entries.reason: Okra, cotton, and roselle share root-knot nematode, Fusarium wilt, and aphid/whitefly pests with cucurbits in warm-climate systems. A 2-year gap, with cucurbits separated as a follow-with crop.
entries.source: UF/IFAS Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

entries.reason: Crops outside the 11 rotation families: perennial fruit, nut trees, asparagus and rhubarb, sweet potato, mushrooms, aquatic crops, medicinal herbs in their own botanical families, ornamental flowers, and fiber/dye crops. Woody perennial trees and shrubs belong here whatever their botany: a family assignment is a claim about what to plant next, and a permanent tree is never a rotation-bed crop, so black locust stays out of legumes and linden out of malvaceae. Bed-grown woody crops keep their family (goji, bamboo). Rotation here is crop-specific: see the per-crop calendar notes.
entries.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension; UC ANR fruit production guides
